translationRepairs: Near the end of the Qianfu reign Xiji entered the jinshi examinations, but with rebellion abroad he fled to Hezhong and entered the service of Military Commissioner Li Du, who raised him to salt-and-iron commissioner.

Near the end of the Qianfu reign Xiji entered the jinshi examinations, but with rebellion abroad he fled to Hezhong and entered the service of Military Commissioner Li Du, who raised him to salt-and-iron judge.
擢為鹽鐵判官 names a salt-and-iron administrative judge, not the commissioner (鹽鐵使). The replacement restores the office without other change.
At the end of the Qianfu era Xiji sat for the jinshi examination; he encountered turmoil, fled to Hezhong, relied on Military Commissioner Li Du, and was promoted to salt-and-iron commissioner.
At the end of the Qianfu era Xiji sat for the jinshi examination; he encountered turmoil, fled to Hezhong, relied on Military Commissioner Li Du, and was promoted to salt-and-iron judge.
The literal likewise renders 判官 as commissioner. Salt-and-iron judge matches the Chinese office.

(Northern Dreams, Trivial Tales: Xiji accompanied Li Keyong to Weinan and was sent to present a memorial at court. The emperor prized his prose, named him Remonstrance Grand Master, and had him report to the northern secretariat as a mark of honor.)〉

(Northern Dreams, Trivial Tales: Xiji accompanied Li Keyong to Weinan and was sent to present a memorial at court. The emperor prized his prose, named him Remonstrance Grand Master, and had him report to the northern secretariat as a mark of honor.)
English already closes the parenthesis; the leftover 〉 is a Chinese annotation closer, not part of the translation.

(Northern Dreams, Trivial Tales: Xiji followed Li Keyong to Weinan; the prince had him enter court with a memorial. The emperor valued his writings, appointed him Remonstrance Grand Master, and had him report to the northern secretariat to honor him.)〉

(Northern Dreams, Trivial Tales: Xiji followed Li Keyong to Weinan; the prince had him enter court with a memorial. The emperor valued his writings, appointed him Remonstrance Grand Master, and had him report to the northern secretariat to honor him.)
The literal sentence likewise ends with a stray Chinese closer after an English parenthesis. Removing it is correct.
Wen Jing raised the Shibi and Bibi tribes; Yuan Hai marched the Five Divisions—with empty boasts they still sometimes won their way.
Wen Jing sought the hosts of Shibi; Yuan Hai marched the Five Divisions—with empty boasts they still sometimes won their way.
文靖求始畢之眾 names only Shibi's hosts and the verb 求 (sought). Bibi is invented; raised is not in the Chinese.
Wen Jing sought the hosts of Shibi and Bibi; Yuan Hai levied the armies of the Five Divisions—with broad words and empty phrases they still sometimes achieved their aim.
Wen Jing sought the hosts of Shibi; Yuan Hai levied the armies of the Five Divisions—with broad words and empty phrases they still sometimes achieved their aim.
The literal also inserts Bibi beside 始畢. Deleting the invented name restores the source.

(New Tang Compendium: Zheng Zhun came from the gentry; before he passed the examinations he served on Shanggu Lian's staff at Jingmen, drafting dispatches that matched the ancients and upholding rectitude without shame before the sages of old. He served as secretary to Cheng Rui, who was enfeoffed as Prince of Shanggu.)〉

(New Tang Compendium: Zheng Zhun came from the gentry; before he passed the examinations he served on the lotus-staff of Shanggu at Jingmen, drafting dispatches that matched the ancients and upholding rectitude without shame before the sages of old. He served as secretary to Cheng Rui, who was enfeoffed as Prince of Shanggu.)〉
上穀蓮幕 is Shanggu's lotus-staff secretariat, later identified as Cheng Rui's. Shanggu Lian is a false personal name.

(New Tang Compendium says: Zheng Zhun, of the gentry class, before passing the examinations assisted Shanggu Lian's Jingmen staff office; in flying letters and running proclamations he yielded to no ancients, upheld rectitude and expelled evil without shame before former sages. Examined: Zhun was secretary to Cheng Rui, and Rui was enfeoffed as Prince of Shanggu Commandery.)〉

(New Tang Compendium says: Zheng Zhun, of the gentry class, before passing the examinations assisted the Shanggu lotus-staff office at Jingmen; in flying letters and running proclamations he yielded to no ancients, upheld rectitude and expelled evil without shame before former sages. Examined: Zhun was secretary to Cheng Rui, and Rui was enfeoffed as Prince of Shanggu Commandery.)〉
The same 蓮幕 phrase is a staff office, not a man named Lian. The proposed literal removes that invention.
In the second year of Tongguang he was posthumously enfeoffed as Minister of Rites.
In the second year of Tongguang he was posthumously granted the office of Minister of Rites.
追贈禮部尚書 is a posthumous grant of office, not a territorial enfeoffment.
Li Jingyi, born Yangu, was a grandson of Grand Preceptor Li Deyu of Wei.
Li Jingyi, originally named Yangu, was a grandson of Grand Commandant and Duke of Wei, Li Deyu.
本名延古 is an original name; 太尉衛公德裕 is Grand Commandant and Duke of Wei, not Grand Preceptor of Wei.

When the rebellions of Huang Chao and Cai Jing engulfed Luoyang, the capital lay in ashes; Quanyi hacked through the ruins to rebuild the city. The Li family's plants were dug up and carted away, sold by woodcutters until the gardens stood bare.

When the rebellions of Huang Chao and Cai engulfed Luoyang, the capital lay in ashes; Quanyi hacked through the ruins to rebuild the city. The Li family's plants were dug up and carted away, sold by woodcutters until the gardens stood bare.
巢、蔡之亂 pairs Huang Chao with the Cai disorders, not a person named Cai Jing.
When Jingyi learned of it he wept and told Quanyi at the Wei River, "At the Pingquan villa my grandfather's admonitions were strict; his unworthy descendants have again broken his will."
When Jingyi learned of it he wept and said to Quanyi, "At the Pingquan villa my grandfather's admonitions were strict; his unworthy descendants have again broken his will."
泣渭全義曰 is 謂 written as 渭: he wept and addressed Quanyi. No Wei River is present; s0113 泣告 confirms speech.
Jingyi learned of it and, weeping, told Quanyi at the Wei: "The Pingquan villa—my grandfather's admonitions were very strict; unworthy descendants constantly violate his intent."
Jingyi learned of it and, weeping, said to Quanyi: "The Pingquan villa—my grandfather's admonitions were very strict; unworthy descendants constantly violate his intent."
The literal's 'at the Wei' likewise misreads 渭 for 謂. Said to Quanyi is the correct sense.
Minister of Works Tu and Li Jingyi have been appointed three times yet nursed their reputation and did not come—all should be removed from office to encourage those who serve their lord."
Sikong Tu and Li Jingyi have been appointed three times yet nursed their reputation and did not come—all should be removed from office to encourage those who serve their lord."
司空圖 is the personal name Sikong Tu, paired with 李敬義, not Minister of Works plus given name Tu.
He must be punished to restore court order; even the Nine Offices' review calls this lenient—demote him to recorder of the Court of the Imperial Stud."
He must be punished to restore court order; even the Nine Offices' review calls this lenient—demote him to recorder of the Court of the Imperial Insignia."
衛尉寺 is the Court of the Imperial Insignia; 太僕寺 would be the Imperial Stud.
Minister of Works Tu also had his prior edict revoked and was allowed to follow leisure as he pleased.
Sikong Tu also had his prior edict revoked and was allowed to follow leisure as he pleased.
s0124 again names 司空圖 as a person; the following 圖，唐史有傳 confirms the given name Tu.

(Old Book of Tang, Annals of Emperor Ai: On the wushen day of the sixth month, an edict demoted former Vice Director Li Yangu, bearer of the crimson fish tally, to recorder of the Court of the Imperial Stud.

(Old Book of Tang, Annals of Emperor Ai: On the wushen day of the sixth month, an edict demoted former Vice Director Li Yangu, bearer of the crimson fish tally, to recorder of the Court of the Imperial Insignia.
The Old Tang annotation repeats 衛尉寺主簿, the insignia court, not the stud.
In the twelfth year Zhuangzong pacified Hebei; when Shi Jiantang took Xinxing, Jingyi came to pay his respects.
In the twelfth year Zhuangzong pacified Hebei; when Shi Jiantang took Xinxiang, Jingyi came to pay his respects.
史建瑭收新鄉 is Xinxiang; Xinxing would be 新興.
In the twelfth year Emperor Zhuangzong pacified Hebei; Shi Jiantang took Xinxing, and Jingyi paid a visit.
In the twelfth year Emperor Zhuangzong pacified Hebei; Shi Jiantang took Xinxiang, and Jingyi paid a visit.
The literal repeats Xinxing for 新鄉. Xinxiang is the required reading.

That year the emperor sent envoys to welcome him to Weizhou, appointed him acting northern capital guardian investigating officer with imperial commission, and enfeoffed him Minister of Works, sending him as envoy to Wang Rong.

That year the emperor sent envoys to welcome him to Weizhou, appointed him acting northern capital guardian investigating officer with imperial commission, appointed him Minister of Works, and sent him as envoy to Wang Rong.
拜工部尚書 is appointment to Minister of Works, not an enfeoffment.

Jingyi's distant ancestors came from Zhao; Wang Rong received him with the courtesy due a fellow townsman, sent his aide Li Zhu with three juan of the Zanhuang Collection, and had him visit the family tombs and steles of earlier generations. When the mission ended, Jingyi returned to duty at Taiyuan.

Because Jingyi's distant ancestors were of Zhao commandery, when he met Rong he displayed the courtesy due a fellow townsman; Rong sent his aide Li Zhu with three juan of the Zanhuang Collection and had him visit the family tombs and steles of earlier generations. When the mission ended, Jingyi returned to duty at Taiyuan.
敬義…見鎔展維桑之敬: Jingyi, meeting Rong, displayed hometown courtesy. The original reverses agent and patient.

Jingyi, because his remote ancestor was of Zhao commandery, when he met Rong received his display of hometown respect; Rong sent his aide Li Zhu with three juan of the Zanhuang Collection, ordering him to visit the tombs and steles of former generations. When the envoy returned, Jingyi resumed duty at Taiyuan.

Jingyi, because his remote ancestors were of Zhao commandery, when he met Rong displayed hometown respect; Rong sent his aide Li Zhu with three juan of the Zanhuang Collection, ordering him to visit the tombs and steles of former generations. When the envoy returned, Jingyi resumed duty at Taiyuan.
The literal makes Rong the one who received the display. Jingyi is the subject of 展.
In the second year of Tongguang he was posthumously enfeoffed as Right Vice Director.
In the second year of Tongguang he was posthumously honored as Right Vice Director.
贈右僕射 is a posthumous honorary office, matching the idiomatic honored, not an enfeoffment.
When Emperor Zhaozong moved east, he was again summoned as Vice Minister of War to Luoyang, was blocked by Liu Can, thanked him once and withdrew.
When Emperor Zhaozong moved east, he was again summoned as Vice Minister of War to Luoyang, was blocked by Liu Can, declined once and withdrew.
一謝而退 is declining or taking leave after being blocked, not thanking Liu Can.
(Xuanhe Calligraphy Catalogue: Rubi, style name Zixie; his grandfather Lun had a poetic name in the Zhenyuan era of Tang.
(Xuanhe Calligraphy Catalogue: Rubi, style name Zixie; his grandfather Lun was famed for poetry in the Zhenyuan era of Tang.
有詩名 means he was famed for poetry in Zhenyuan, not that he possessed a poetic name.
He died at Jinyang before the founding of the dynasty.
He died in Jin before the founding of the dynasty.
卒於晉 names Jin, not Jinyang (晉陽). The idiomatic place is an invention.
(Xuanhe Calligraphy Catalogue: posthumously enfeoffed Minister of War.)〉
(Xuanhe Calligraphy Catalogue: posthumously honored as Minister of War.)〉
贈兵部尚書 is a posthumous honor, not an enfeoffment.
He was posthumously enfeoffed Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
He was posthumously honored as Junior Mentor of the Heir Apparent.
贈太子少保 is likewise a posthumous honorary office, not an enfeoffment.
The next year the Liang Founder forced the abdication; Xun was deputy envoy for the enfeoffment rites.
The next year the Liang Founder forced the abdication; Xun was deputy envoy for the investiture rites.
冊禮副使 in 梁祖逼禪 is the accession investiture, not a grant of land.

An edict declared, "Su Kai, Lu Geng, and four others wrote the meanest verse, piled redundancy upon redundancy, had no learning yet stole degrees, and stained the court's fairness—they are struck from the rolls and barred from the examination grounds forever."

An edict declared, "Su Kai, Lu Geng, and two others—four men in all—wrote the meanest verse, piled redundancy upon redundancy, had no learning yet stole degrees, and stained the court's fairness—they are struck from the rolls and barred from the examination grounds forever."
蘇楷、盧賡等四人 is four men in all, including the two named, not two plus four others.

Minister of Ceremonies Zhang Tingfan submitted: "Zhaozong at first showed true sagely virtue, but later his glory faded; Ji kept him captive and Maozhen seized the court—though ill fortune pressed him repeatedly, he also lost the Way from first to last.

Minister of Ceremonies Zhang Tingfan submitted: "Zhaozong at first showed true sagely virtue, but later his glory faded; Jishu kept him captive and Maozhen seized the imperial progress—though ill fortune pressed him repeatedly, he also lost the Way from first to last.
季述 is Jishu; 劫幸 is seizure of the imperial progress, not a truncated Ji or a generic court.
I request the posthumous title Respectful, Spirited, Solemn, Sorrowful Emperor and the temple name Emperor Xiang."
I request the posthumous title Respectful, Spirited, Solemn, Sorrowful Emperor and the temple name Xiangzong."
廟號襄宗 is the temple name Xiangzong, not a separate Emperor Xiang.
In the second year of Tongguang he was posthumously enfeoffed Left Vice Director, and Kai was made Vice Director.
In the second year of Tongguang he was posthumously granted Left Vice Director, and Kai was made Vice Director.
贈左僕射 is a posthumous office grant for Su Xun, not an enfeoffment.
